title: Do Verifiers Reduce Security-Relevant Misconfigurations? A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Verifier-in-the-Loop GVR for Intent-to-Configuration
abstract: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired experiment (N = 300 matched intents) to test whether embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline. Under a frozen adapter contract that used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (one LLM candidate replayed to both arms to conserve provider calls), the run completed all planned episodes (600 episodes; model_calls_used = 300). Both baseline and guarded arms passed the forbidden-reachability predicate on all 300 pairs (n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0). Paired risk-difference = 0.0, exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Because validators never flagged violations, no repair calls were invoked and the preregistered confirmatory hypothesis about repair efficacy was untestable in this run. Observing 0/300 violations yields a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound ≈ 0.00994 on the baseline violation rate. We present artifact-grounded interpretation, explain how generation semantics and adversary strength constrained inferential power, and archive the preregistration and deterministic per-episode traces to support reproducible follow-up stress tests that explicitly exercise the repair path.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation with large language models (LLMs) promises operational efficiency but raises safety concerns: misconfigurations can expand attack surface or violate access policies. Research therefore advocates constrained generation, execution-oracle checks, and iterative generate–verify–repair (GVR) loops to mitigate such risks [10, 11]. Prior work demonstrates that verifier feedback can materially improve generated-artifact correctness in code and infrastructure tasks, but rigorous, preregistered evidence that a verifier-in-the-loop reduces security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations under adversarial inputs for NetOps is limited.

This paper reports a preregistered paired experiment that directly addresses the operational question: Does embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a GVR loop reduce the incidence of forbidden-reachability misconfigurations from an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline? We executed a deterministic Dockerized emulation with two deterministic validators combined by logical OR, a matched sample of N = 300 intents (150 benign + 150 adversarial variants), and a shared_initial_candidate generation contract to conserve model calls. Our contributions are (1) a transparent, machine-readable preregistration and deterministic execution manifest for a paired confirmatory design (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1); (2) an artifact-backed report of a degenerate but informative empirical outcome (n11 = 300) with exact paired accounting and descriptive bounds on undetected baseline violation rate; (3) concise methodological clarification of the forbidden-reachability predicate and the validators used; and (4) evidence-grounded design lessons for follow-up stress tests that can exercise the repair path.
sections.related_work: Generate–verify–repair and execution-guided repair architectures have improved correctness for code and IaC tasks by using verifier feedback to guide repairs; empirical gains depend on verifier power and repair design [10]. Surveys and NetOps system studies document LLM failure modes (hallucination, overconfidence, domain mismatch) and recommend validators, constrained generation, or human oversight for operational risk control [11,12]. Emulation and testbed research demonstrates that execution-based validation is practical for research-grade evaluation while also warning that emulators and synthetic tasks have external-validity limits relative to production networks [13]. Our study narrows a concrete evidence gap: a preregistered, paired confirmatory evaluation with deterministic per-episode validator traces and explicit generation semantics accounting.
sections.methodology:
Design and preregistration: The preregistered design (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) specified a paired binary confirmatory experiment with N = 300 matched intents (150 benign seeds and 150 deterministic adversarial variants), primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, and a McNemar paired test (alpha = 0.05). Sampling, deduplication (exact and fuzzy dedupe with normalized edit-distance threshold 0.15), exclusion rules, and sensitivity analyses were fixed in the preregistration. The preregistration, adapter contract, and execution manifest are archived in the evidence bundle.

Generation semantics and adapter contract: To limit provider usage we executed a shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each matched intent pair, the pipeline generated one initial LLM candidate which was replayed identically to both experimental arms (baseline = replay; guarded = same candidate validated and repaired if a validator triggered). This choice yields exactly one hosted-model generation per pair (model_calls_used = 300 for 300 pairs) rather than two independent draws per pair (maximum_model_calls = 600 allowed by the contract). The shared-replay semantics reduce between-arm sampling variance and therefore reduce the chance of producing discordant pairs that would exercise the repair path; we make that trade-off explicit because it directly affects inferential power.

Definition of forbidden-reachability predicate and validators: For this study the forbidden-reachability predicate is a deterministic, configuration-level policy violation test: a candidate is flagged if applying the candidate to the emulator produces any policy-violating reachability or otherwise violates declared workflow policies in the task manifest (notably exposures involving declared protected interfaces such as 'mgmt1' or violation of per-task 'workflow_policies' that the task generator includes). In practice the two deterministic validators were (a) a containerized execution-style validator (Batfish-style) that applies a candidate configuration to the emulated FRRouting-style environment and evaluates reachability/policy queries, and (b) a lightweight graph-based static reachability analyzer implemented in Python that computes deterministic reachability consequences from parsed configuration state. The study combined the two validators with a logical-OR rule: a pair is labeled violating if either validator reports forbidden reachability. Validator identifiers and versions are recorded per episode as validator_id = 'deterministic_netops_validator_v5' and validator_version = '5.0'.

Intervention and repair policy: Baseline = replay of the shared initial candidate. Guarded = the same candidate subjected to validator checks; if any validator reported forbidden reachability the preregistered repair policy allowed up to one repair LLM call to produce a corrected candidate, after which validators rechecked the repaired output. Repair was prespecified to be triggered only by validator-detected forbidden reachability and limited to one repair call per pair. All repair invocation logic and prompt templates are archived in the transformation manifest.

Execution environment and determinism: Experiments ran in deterministic Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation with fixed seeds and deterministic task generation. Per-episode raw responses, validator traces, provider-call audit, and deterministic reconciliation records were archived to enable replay. The final CI estimation used bootstrap percentile CIs with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729); this resampling increase from the preregistered 1,000 resamples is recorded and disclosed in the analysis log.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: Planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs × 2 arms); completed = 600; failed episodes = 0. Provider-call accounting under the shared_initial_candidate contract: model_calls_used = 300 (stage_counts: 'shared_initial_generation' = 300). The run interval and these counts are recorded in the execution manifest.

Primary confirmatory outcome: Every matched pair passed the forbidden-reachability predicate in both arms. Contingency counts are n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (Table 1). The paired risk-difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. The prespecified bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) for the paired risk-difference is [0.0, 0.0]. Because no initial candidates were flagged, no repair calls were invoked and all per-episode validator_trace.repair_applied flags are false.

Descriptive bound on undetected baseline violations: Observing 0/300 violations provides a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound on the true baseline violation probability of 1 − 0.05^(1/300) ≈ 0.00994 (≈0.994%). We report this numeric bound as the strict descriptive constraint that the run places on the baseline violation rate under the evaluated model, validators, emulator, and task-selection procedure.

Interpretation of degenerate contingency: The primary confirmatory hypothesis prespecified reduction in violation proportion via repair. That hypothesis is untestable here because two coupled design outcomes occurred: (1) the shared_initial_candidate replay semantics reduced independent-sample variability across arms (baseline was not an independent draw), and (2) none of the programmatic adversarial variants produced any validator-detectable forbidden reachability for the declared model and validators. The McNemar test requires discordant pairs (n10 or n01) to measure paired differences; with n10 = n01 = 0 the paired test is uninformative about repair efficacy. The artifact bundle (per-episode scoring files and the paired contingency table) documents these facts.
sections.discussion:
What the evidence supports: Under the exact adapter contract, declared model (gpt-5-mini), validator set (two deterministic validators combined by logical OR), emulator, and the programmatic adversarial perturbation generator used here, initial LLM candidates satisfied the forbidden-reachability predicate on all sampled intents; therefore inserting a verifier did not change observed compliance. The deterministic artifact record supports this narrow, concrete conclusion: provider-call accounting, per-episode validator traces, and the paired contingency are mutually consistent.

What the evidence does not support: The experiment provides no evidence that verifier-guided repair can rescue violating initial candidates because the repair path was never invoked. The preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and targeted detecting a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction; the observed degenerate contingency violates that assumption and renders the confirmatory test moot for repair efficacy.

Design lessons and operational recommendations (artifact-grounded): (1) Generation semantics matter: shared_initial_candidate reduces model calls but also reduces between-arm variance needed to produce discordant violations. For experiments intended to test repair efficacy we recommend independent-condition generation (two independent LLM draws per matched intent) or enlarged repair budgets; the execution manifest records the model-call budget trade-off (maximum_model_calls = 600) so practitioners can plan provider costs. (2) Adversary potency matters: the deterministic adversarial perturbations used here (one variant per benign seed) did not trigger validator-detectable forbidden reachability; stronger adversaries targeted at the verifier predicate are necessary to exercise repair. (3) Verifier diversity and oracle strength matter: combining multiple verifier families and including higher-fidelity execution oracles will increase construct coverage of operational risk. (4) Reproducibility is practical: the archived per-episode raw responses, validator traces, provider-call audit, and analysis logs permit exact reanalysis and targeted follow-up runs that change only generation semantics, adversary strength, or model selection.

Threats to validity: Internal validity is constrained by shared_initial_candidate semantics and single-model scope. Construct validity depends on whether the forbidden-reachability predicate and the two deterministic validators adequately capture operational security risk; validator IDs and versions are archived for independent assessment (validator_id = 'deterministic_netops_validator_v5', validator_version = '5.0'). External validity is limited by synthetic tasks and Dockerized emulation; results do not necessarily generalize to production devices or live traffic. Conclusion validity is limited because the observed contingency is degenerate and the preregistered power assumptions do not hold. We enumerate these threats so subsequent stress tests can be targeted.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired experiment to evaluate a verifier-in-the-loop GVR pipeline for intent→configuration generation. Under the executed adapter contract (shared_initial_candidate), declared model (gpt-5-mini), two deterministic validators combined by logical OR, and the sampled task set, both baseline and guarded arms passed the forbidden-reachability predicate on all 300 matched intents; consequently the preregistered confirmatory test of repair efficacy was untestable because no discordant pairs occurred. The run nonetheless places a strict descriptive bound (one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound ≈ 0.00994) on the undetected baseline violation rate under the evaluated conditions and yields concrete design lessons: generation semantics, adversary strength, repair budgeting, and verifier diversity materially affect whether a verifier-in-the-loop architecture can be empirically shown to reduce security-relevant misconfigurations. We release the preregistration, execution manifest, per-episode validator traces, raw responses, and analysis artifacts to enable reproducible follow-up stress tests that intentionally exercise the repair path (independent draws, stronger adversaries, multi-model comparisons, richer oracles).

limitations: Degenerate confirmatory outcome: zero discordant pairs (n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0) render the McNemar paired test uninformative about repair efficacy because the repair path was never exercised.

GVR repair not evaluated: because validators never flagged violations, no repair calls were invoked; the experiment thus tests whether verifier insertion changes compliance when baseline is already compliant, not whether verifier-guided repair rescues violations.

Generation-contract choice: shared_initial_candidate reduced model-call overhead (model_calls_used = 300) but also limited independent draws that could produce discordant errors; independent-condition generation or expanded repair budgets are recommended for follow-up tests.

Adversarial-perturbation potency: the deterministic programmatic adversarial variants used did not trigger validator-detectable forbidden reachability for the evaluated model and validators; stronger, targeted adversaries are needed to exercise repair.

External validity: tasks were synthetically generated and executed in Dockerized emulation; outcomes do not necessarily generalize to heterogeneous production devices, live traffic, or different operational constraints.
Model and verifier scope: a single declared model (gpt-5-mini) and two deterministic validators were evaluated; results may differ for other LLMs, verifier families, or higher-fidelity oracles.
